newsitem.title: USA: Exile boats, planes hold protest off Cuban coast.
newsitem.headline: Exile boats, planes hold protest off Cuban coast.

text.p: Cuban exiles held a peaceful demonstration off Cuba's north coast on Saturday to promote a national work stoppage on the Communist-ruled island.
A dozen boats and a few planes gathered near Cuba's 12-mile territorial waters limit off Havana, where crewmembers held a prayer service and then turned back to Florida.
The flotilla was far smaller than the Cuban exile group Democracy Movement had intended and the first of three planned before Pope John Paul's visit to Cuba in early 1998.
It was the latest in a series of flotillas mounted by Miami-based Cuban exiles that have served to heighten tension between the United States and Fidel Castro's Communist regime.

In Havana, Cuban media said navy vessels monitored the flotilla from inside Cuban territorial waters, but there were no incidents. The official Prensa Latina news agency said the flotilla stopped two miles outside Cuban territory.
Cuban journalists aboard a submarine chaser that observed the demonstration from two miles inside the 12-mile limit said the flotilla consisted of eight boats and two planes.
Democracy Movement organisers said 12 boats and seven planes took part in the protest.
Cuba on Thursday described the flotilla as a "new attempt at a provocation" and said it would use "the necessary means" to ensure there were no violations of its territory.
Democracy Movement had assured U.S. and Cuban authorities it did not intend to enter Cuban waters.
Organisers said at least three dozen vessels set out from the Florida Keys. But rough seas and thunderstorms forced some of the boats to abandon the trip, the U.S. Coast Guard said.
"They ran into a little weather problem," Coast Guard spokesman Scott Carr said. "We haven't heard any reports of trouble," Carr said. "They're heading back."

Miami-based Cuban exiles have sent a number of flotillas across the Florida Straits between Florida and Cuba. During one in 1995, a Democracy Movement boat entered Cuban waters and was sideswiped by Cuban military vessels.
In February 1996, Cuban MiG fighter jets shot down two unarmed U.S. civilian planes between Florida and Cuba, killing four aviators of the exile group Brothers to the Rescue.

The incident provoked international outrage against Cuba. But President Fidel Castro's government defended its action by saying the planes were violating its territory. Washington said the downed planes were outside Cuban airspace and should not have been shot down.

Democracy Movement said Saturday's flotilla was aimed at publicising within Cuba the idea of a general strike at an as- yet-undetermined date. The group espouses nonviolent protest with the aim of stirring democratic reforms in Cuba.
Democracy Movement leaders have said they reserve their right as Cuban citizens to enter Cuban territory at any time and intend to exercise that right during the pope's visit.
